summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Federal courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub in Barra Bonita that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Maranhão is one of Brazil's 27 states and sits entirely inside that national framework. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Lethal violence is the dominant practical finding. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil during 2025, a fall of about 34 per cent year-on-year, and records Brazil first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Maranhão accounted for 5 of those 80 killings.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, and documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units. The study treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights.
tangentialFactors:
Brazil has led the world rankings for killings of trans people for years. CNN Brasil reported on 27 January 2025 that ANTRA's dossier for that year counted 122 trans and travesti people killed in 2024, a sixteenth consecutive year at the top of the global ranking and 16 per cent below 2023; victims were mostly young, Black women, many from the Northeast, and the crimes were marked by extreme violence. Maranhão lies in that region, which sharpens the exposure of trans people there even as the 2025 national total fell.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists.

Political participation has grown alongside the threats. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.
localsOnly:
Residents serving sentences are the group for whom the placement rules bite hardest, and the record on their day-to-day rights rests on older instruments. An online encyclopedia's account of LGBTI prisoner rights states that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons separate from other prisoners, that transsexuals have the right to be called by their social name rather than their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons, and that LGBTQ people in prisons may choose male or female clothing. That passage is footnoted to a G1 report of 17 April 2014 on a federal portaria granting rights to gay and travesti prisoners.

The 2021 Rio de Janeiro census study also records a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting travestis and trans women parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, alongside national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Protection machinery has widened for residents. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the federal portaria behind the prisoner-rights description is unresolved. The claim traces to a G1 report dated 17 April 2014, archived 12 July 2018, and was not independently re-verified against the instrument as it stands now, so its present force should be treated as unconfirmed rather than as established current law.

A second online encyclopedia overview of LGBTQ people in prison, fetched 4 October 2026, carries no trans-prisoner placement rule for Brazil in its transgender section; that section discusses only social vulnerability, stigma and fragmented identity among travestis and transgender people during rehabilitation, while placement norms are documented for other countries. No independent corroboration of a Brazil-specific placement rule was located in that source.

No Maranhão-specific enforcement data, facility-level account, or state legislative measure on gender identity or LGBTI protection appears in the sources reviewed; the only Maranhão figure carried here is the count of 5 trans and travesti people killed out of the national 80 for 2025. Whether Maranhão applies the National Council of Justice placement resolutions through any state-level directive is not sourced.
